claim: Human H3N2 influenza nucleoprotein accumulates roughly one amino-acid substitution per year.
source_text: Although NP's evolution is less rapid and medically infamous than that of its surface counterparts hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, NP still accumulates roughly one amino-acid substitution per year (Rambaut et al., 2008).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by a citation to Rambaut et al., 2008.

claim: Nucleoprotein's primary function is serving as a scaffold for viral RNA during transcription and genome packaging.
source_text: Crucially for our experiment, NP's primary function—serving as a scaffold for viral RNA during transcription and genome packaging (Portela and Digard, 2002; Ye et al., 2006)—occurs within the interior of infected cells
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Portela and Digard, 2002 and Ye et al., 2006.

claim: Nucleoprotein is a target of cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
source_text: NP is also a target of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), and so is under continual pressure for change in CTL epitopes (Berkhoff et al., 2004, 2007; Valkenburg et al., 2011)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Berkhoff et al., 2004, 2007 and Valkenburg et al., 2011.

claim: The evolutionary trajectory from Aichi/1968 to Brisbane/2007 NP involves 39 mutations.
source_text: We focused on the evolutionary trajectory separating NPs from two human H3N2 strains isolated 39 years apart, A/Aichi/2/1968 and A/Brisbane/10/2007
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the authors' reconstruction of the evolutionary trajectory shown in Figure 2.

claim: Three mutations (L259S, R348G, and V280A) are deleterious to the parent Aichi/1968 NP despite becoming fixed during evolution.
source_text: Most single mutants were highly functional, but three (L259S, R384G, V280A) exhibited large decreases in activity.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of transcriptional activity shown in Figure 3B.

claim: L259S, R384G, and V280A reduce viral growth by more than 20-fold.
source_text: Viruses with the parent (Aichi/1968) or final (Brisbane/2007) NP grew to comparably high titers in tissue culture (Figure 3C), but growth of the three transcriptionally impaired mutants was dramatically lower (>1000-fold lower for L259S and R384G, and >20-fold lower for V280A).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental viral growth assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: N334H rescues the deleterious effects of L259S on transcriptional activity and viral growth.
source_text: L259S impairs the transcriptional activity and viral growth of both the parent Aichi/1968 and the evolutionary intermediate Step 10, but is rescued by N334H in both backgrounds.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The reversion of L259S preceded R384G in the evolutionary trajectory and plays an important role in enabling R384G.
source_text: The reversion of L259S that preceded Step 21 plays an important role in enabling R384G, as the evolutionary intermediate without this reversion (Step 20) is more negatively affected by R384G.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing the effects of R384G in different evolutionary intermediates shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M136I largely rescues the deleterious effect of V280A.
source_text: M136I, which immediately preceded V280A in the natural evolution, mostly rescues its deleterious effect in the background of Aichi/1968 (Figure 4C).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The epistatically interacting residues are not in contact in the monomeric or known oligomeric NP crystal structures.
source_text: None of the identified epistatically interacting residues are in contact in the monomeric or known oligomeric NP crystal structures
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: N334H rescues the transcriptional activity of all three individually deleterious mutations (L259S, R384G, V280A).
source_text: N334H rescues activity for each of these mutations
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The three individually deleterious mutations (L259S, R384G, V280A) reduce NP protein levels in transfected cells.
source_text: Western blot showing that the three individually deleterious mutations all reduce NP levels in transfected cells relative to an mCherry control expressed from an IRES in the same plasmid; this effect is counteracted by N334H.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C and quantified in Figure 6D.

claim: L259S, R384G, and V280A are destabilizing mutations with changes in melting temperatures ranging from −3.6°C to −4.9°C.
source_text: The three individually deleterious mutations were all destabilizing, with changes in melting temperatures (ΔTm) relative to the parent Aichi/1968 NP that ranged from −3.6°C to −4.9°C.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by circular dichroism thermal denaturation experiments shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplements 4–6.

claim: N334H is a stabilizing mutation with a ΔTm of 4.4°C.
source_text: N334H was stabilizing (ΔTm of 4.4°C), and adding N334H to each of the individual destabilized mutants restored their stability to roughly wild-type values (Figure 6E).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by circular dichroism thermal denaturation experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: M136I is a modestly stabilizing mutation.
source_text: M136I is also modestly stabilizing, and partially rescues all three individually deleterious mutations (Figure 6—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by circular dichroism thermal denaturation experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 4–7.

claim: NP stability above a threshold of approximately 42°C is neutral with respect to transcriptional activity.
source_text: As long as the stability is greater than a threshold around 42°C, changes in stability are neutral with respect to activity. Below this threshold, activity declines sharply with decreasing stability.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by the relationship between stability and activity shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The parent Aichi/1968 NP is only marginally more stable than the minimal threshold where activity and viral growth begin to suffer.
source_text: The parent Aichi/1968 is only marginally more stable than the minimal threshold where activity and viral growth begin to suffer.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the stability measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: All three destabilizing mutations (L259S, R384G, V280A) occur in characterized CTL epitopes.
source_text: All three destabilizing mutations occur in characterized epitopes (DiBrino et al., 1995; Voeten et al., 2000; Rimmelzwaan et al., 2004b; Berkhoff et al., 2007; Assarsson et al., 2008; Alexander et al., 2010; Cheung et al., 2012)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that characterized CTL epitopes.

claim: Mutations at two of the three destabilizing sites have been shown to reduce CTL recognition.
source_text: mutations at two of these sites have been shown to reduce CTL recognition (Voeten et al., 2000; Berkhoff et al., 2004; Rimmelzwaan et al., 2004b; Berkhoff et al., 2007; Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing reduced CTL recognition.

claim: The three epistatically constrained mutations are significantly enriched in CTL epitopes relative to all sites in NP (p=0.001).
source_text: Sites 259, 280, and 384 are in significantly more epitopes than three random positions from all sites (p=0.001)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of epitope data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The three epistatically constrained mutations are significantly enriched in CTL epitopes relative to sites that experienced substitutions along the evolutionary trajectory (p=0.004).
source_text: Sites 259, 280, and 384 are in significantly more epitopes than three random positions from all sites (p=0.001) or the mutated sites (p=0.004)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of epitope data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Stabilizing mutations enable NP to tolerate otherwise deleterious destabilizing mutations.
source_text: These stabilizing mutations enable NP to tolerate otherwise deleterious destabilizing mutations.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that stabilizing mutations rescue the effects of destabilizing mutations.

claim: Stability-mediated epistasis constrains NP's adaptation as well as its sequence evolution.
source_text: Stability-mediated epistasis therefore constrains NP's adaptation as well as its sequence evolution, since the accessibility of immune-escape mutations is dependent on the acquisition of enabling mutations.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that destabilizing immune-escape mutations require prior stabilizing mutations.

claim: Most of the intermediates during NP's evolution are only marginally more stable than the minimal threshold where function begins to suffer.
source_text: As shown in Figure 7C, most of the intermediates during NP's evolution are only marginally more stable than the minimal threshold where function begins to suffer.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by stability measurements of evolutionary intermediates shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Higher stability has no deleterious effect on NP function.
source_text: Our results decisively favor the second explanation for NP, since the evolving protein is usually marginally stable despite the fact that higher stability has no deleterious effect (Figure 7A,B).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by the data in Figure 7A,B showing that increased stability does not impair activity or growth.

claim: The stabilizing M136I preceded the destabilizing V280A in the evolutionary trajectory.
source_text: The stabilizing M136I preceded V280A, and provided a stability cushion to eliminate V280A's otherwise deleterious effect (Figures 4C, 7C).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory and experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 7C.

claim: The stabilizing S259L preceded the destabilizing R384G in the evolutionary trajectory.
source_text: The stabilizing S259L preceded the destabilizing R384G, and was necessary (in conjunction with E375G) to alleviate R384G's otherwise deleterious effect (Figures 4B, 7C).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory and experimental data shown in Figures 4B and 7C.

claim: E375G is necessary in conjunction with S259L to fully rescue the growth defect of R384G.
source_text: The further addition of E375G to Step 21 containing R384G eliminates the remaining growth impairment—but E375G alone fails to rescue R384G in the background of Aichi/1968 (Figure 4B).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The deleterious effects of L259S, R348G, and V280A are not caused by the genetic background of influenza polymerase proteins.
source_text: The deleterious effects on activity caused by L259S, R348G, and V280A are not caused by the genetic background of influenza polymerase proteins, as these three mutants are impaired regardless of whether the polymerase proteins are derived from Nanchang/1995, Aichi/1968, or Brisbane/2007 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data testing the mutations in different polymerase backgrounds shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: All NP evolutionary intermediates tested are functional in a fixed background of other proteins.
source_text: There is also the potential for epistasis between NP and other viral proteins, although we see no evidence for such epistasis here, since all NP evolutionary intermediates that we tested are functional in a fixed background of other proteins.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the experimental observation that all tested intermediates showed activity in the assays with fixed polymerase proteins.

claim: Stability-mediated epistasis is the dominant constraint on NP evolution.
source_text: But doubtless some of these other mechanisms of epistasis would become apparent if we examined even longer evolutionary trajectories. However, the overriding message from our experiments is that stability-mediated epistasis is the dominant constraint on NP evolution.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is inferred from the comprehensive experimental data showing that most observed epistatic effects can be explained by protein stability.

claim: The evolutionary trajectory was reconstructed using 431 date-stamped human H3N2 NP protein sequences.
source_text: Via Markov chain Monte Carlo implemented in BEAST (Drummond et al., 2012), we estimated the joint posterior distribution of phylogenetic trees and mutations along the branches of these trees given 431 date-stamped human H3N2 NP protein sequences from the Influenza Virus Resource.
evidence_reasoning: The claim describes the data used for the phylogenetic reconstruction.

claim: NP's primary function occurs within the interior of infected cells and is fairly authentically represented in tissue-culture assays.
source_text: Crucially for our experiment, NP's primary function—serving as a scaffold for viral RNA during transcription and genome packaging (Portela and Digard, 2002; Ye et al., 2006)—occurs within the interior of infected cells, and so is probably fairly authentically represented in tissue-culture assays.
evidence_reasoning: The claim combines established knowledge about NP function with an inference about the validity of tissue culture assays.

claim: CTL selection in influenza is thought to be weaker than antibody selection on the viral surface proteins.
source_text: CTL selection in influenza is thought to be weaker than antibody selection on the viral surface proteins, and so much of NP's evolution is shaped by stochastic forces such as population bottlenecks and hitchhiking with antigenic mutations in the surface proteins (Rambaut et al., 2008; Bhatt et al., 2011)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Rambaut et al., 2008 and Bhatt et al., 2011.

claim: Some CTL epitopes in NP are under functional constraint.
source_text: a pressure partially countered by the fact that some of these epitopes are under functional constraint (Rimmelzwaan, et al., 2004a; Berkhoff et al., 2005, 2006).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Rimmelzwaan et al., 2004a and Berkhoff et al., 2005, 2006.

claim: Epistasis can constrain accessible evolutionary pathways.
source_text: Epistasis can play a key role in evolution, such as by constraining accessible evolutionary pathways (Weinreich et al., 2005; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2011)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Weinreich et al., 2005 and Kryazhimskiy et al., 2011.

claim: Epistasis can increase the role of contingency in adaptation.
source_text: Epistasis can play a key role in evolution, such as by constraining accessible evolutionary pathways (Weinreich et al., 2005; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2011) and increasing the role of contingency in adaptation (Blount et al., 2008; Bridgham et al., 2009).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Blount et al., 2008 and Bridgham et al., 2009.

claim: Laboratory evolution and site-directed mutagenesis experiments have demonstrated that mutations can exhibit strong epistatic interactions.
source_text: But although numerous laboratory evolution and site-directed mutagenesis experiments have demonstrated that mutations can in principle exhibit strong epistatic interactions (Bershtein et al., 2006; Bloom et al., 2006; Lunzer et al., 2010; Salverda et al., 2011)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to multiple laboratory studies.

claim: Studies of antibiotic resistance and steroid-receptor ligand specificity have found strong epistatic interactions.
source_text: A few studies have reconstructed naturally occurring mutations involved in antibiotic resistance or steroid-receptor ligand specificity (Wang et al., 2002; Weinreich et al., 2006; Ortlund et al., 2007; Bridgham et al., 2009) and found strong epistatic interactions.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2002; Weinreich et al., 2006; Ortlund et al., 2007; and Bridgham et al., 2009.

claim: The actual temporal order of mutations in most previous epistasis studies is unknown.
source_text: However, these studies have focused on small numbers of mutations pre-selected for analysis due to their putative adaptive role, and in most cases the actual temporal order of mutations is unknown.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on a review of previous studies and identifies a limitation in the existing literature.

claim: E375G has been previously reported to partially compensate for R384G in slightly different genetic backgrounds.
source_text: Note that E375G has also been previously reported to partially compensate for R384G in slightly different genetic backgrounds (Rimmelzwaan et al., 2004a).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by a citation to Rimmelzwaan et al., 2004a.

claim: Stabilizing mutations have been identified as contributing to the evolution of enzyme specificities.
source_text: Previous experimental studies have identified stabilizing mutations as contributing to the evolution of enzyme specificities (Bloom et al., 2006)
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by a citation to Bloom et al., 2006.

claim: Stabilizing mutations contribute to bacterial and viral drug resistance.
source_text: Previous experimental studies have identified stabilizing mutations as contributing to the evolution of enzyme specificities (Bloom et al., 2006), bacterial (Wang et al., 2002; Bershtein et al., 2006; Weinreich et al., 2006) and viral (Chang and Torbett, 2011) drug resistance
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on drug resistance.

claim: Stabilizing mutations contribute to H5N1 transmissibility.
source_text: Previous experimental studies have identified stabilizing mutations as contributing to the evolution of enzyme specificities (Bloom et al., 2006), bacterial (Wang et al., 2002; Bershtein et al., 2006; Weinreich et al., 2006) and viral (Chang and Torbett, 2011) drug resistance, and H5N1 transmissibility (Imai et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by a citation to Imai et al., 2012.

claim: It is common for mutations to be deleterious to one protein homolog but benign to another.
source_text: At a broader level, analyses of large datasets have shown that it is common for mutations to be deleterious to one protein homolog but benign to another (Kondrashov et al., 2002; Baresic et al., 2010).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by citations to Kondrashov et al., 2002 and Baresic et al., 2010.

claim: The marginal stability of natural proteins has been noted previously.
source_text: This marginal stability of natural proteins has been noted previously, and been given two distinct explanations.
evidence_reasoning: The claim refers to established observations in the scientific literature about protein stability.

claim: One explanation for marginal protein stability is that evolution actively selects for marginal stability because both insufficient and excess stability are deleterious.
source_text: The first explanation holds that evolution actively selects for marginal stability because both insufficient and excess stability are deleterious (DePristo et al., 2005; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009).
evidence_reasoning: The claim describes a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations to DePristo et al., 2005 and Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009.

claim: An alternative explanation for marginal protein stability is that evolution only selects against insufficient stability, and extra stability is rapidly eroded by functionally neutral but destabilizing mutations.
source_text: The second explanation holds that evolution only selects against insufficient stability, but that proteins typically are marginally stable because most mutations are destabilizing and so extra stability is rapidly eroded by functionally neutral but destabilizing mutations (Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Bloom et al., 2007).
evidence_reasoning: The claim describes an alternative hypothesis from the literature supported by citations to Taverna and Goldstein, 2002 and Bloom et al., 2007.

claim: The results favor the explanation that evolution only selects against insufficient stability for NP.
source_text: Our results decisively favor the second explanation for NP, since the evolving protein is usually marginally stable despite the fact that higher stability has no deleterious effect (Figure 7A,B).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that increased stability does not impair function.

claim: The antigenic evolution of influenza hemagglutinin is punctuated.
source_text: For example, the antigenic evolution of influenza hemagglutinin is punctuated, with a fairly constant rate of sequence change nonetheless leading to periodic jumps in antigenicity that require reformulation of the annual influenza vaccine (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2004.

claim: One explanation for punctuated antigenic evolution is that adaptive antigenic change is limited by the waiting time for antigenically neutral mutations that can be productively combined with mutations causing large antigenic changes.
source_text: One explanation that has been posited for this punctuated pattern is that adaptive antigenic change is limited not by the overall rate of substitution, but rather by the waiting time for the protein to accumulate antigenically neutral mutations that can be productively combined with mutations causing large antigenic changes (Koelle et al., 2006; van Nimwegen, 2006).
evidence_reasoning: The claim describes a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations to Koelle et al., 2006 and van Nimwegen, 2006.

claim: Functionally neutral but stabilizing mutations occasionally fix by stochastic forces such as genetic drift, population bottlenecks, or hitchhiking.
source_text: We therefore suggest the following: functionally neutral but stabilizing mutations occasionally fix by stochastic forces such as genetic drift, population bottlenecks, or hitchhiking.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental results and evolutionary theory.

claim: The three destabilizing mutations identified are adaptive since they contribute to viral immune escape.
source_text: Although these destabilizing mutations could in principle also fix by stochastic forces, the three that we have identified are actually adaptive since they contribute to viral immune escape.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is inferred from the enrichment of these mutations in CTL epitopes and literature evidence of reduced CTL recognition.

claim: L259S and N334H fixed in an unknown order in evolutionary intermediate Step 10.
source_text: L259S fixed in an unknown order with another mutation (N334H) in an evolutionary intermediate that we have labeled Step 10
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory which could not resolve the order of these mutations.

claim: R384G fixed in Step 21 in an unknown order with several other mutations.
source_text: The next individually deleterious mutation, R384G, fixed in Step 21 in an unknown order with several other mutations (Figure 4B).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory shown in Figure 4B.

claim: L259S reverted in the transition from Step 20 to Step 21.
source_text: Immediately prior to this, the individually deleterious mutation L259S reverted in the transition from Step 20 to Step 21.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory.

claim: V280A fixed in evolutionary intermediate Step 35.
source_text: The final individually deleterious mutation, V280A, fixed in Step 35.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory.

claim: M136I immediately preceded V280A in the natural evolution.
source_text: M136I, which immediately preceded V280A in the natural evolution, mostly rescues its deleterious effect in the background of Aichi/1968 (Figure 4C).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the reconstructed evolutionary trajectory shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The final Brisbane/2007 NP contains two of the three identified destabilizing mutations (V280A and R384G) and both identified stabilizing mutations (N334H and M136I).
source_text: The final Brisbane/2007 NP contains two of the three identified destabilizing mutations (L259S reverts) and both of the identified stabilizing mutations—combining all four mutations in the parental Aichi/1968 background gives wild-type levels of activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 8).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on sequence comparison and experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 8.

claim: An NP with V280A, R384G, N334H, and M136I exhibits wild-type levels of activity.
source_text: The final NP variant at the end of the trajectory contained V280A, R384G, N334H, and M136I—but not L259S, as this mutation reverts before the occurrence of R384G. An NP with just those four mutations exhibits wild-type levels of activity.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 8.

claim: R384 and E375 are on the same surface of NP, contributing positive and negative charges respectively.
source_text: R384 and E375 are on the same surface, contributing positive and negative charges. Mutating both to neutral glycine maintains the net charge.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on analysis of the NP crystal structure and basic knowledge of amino acid properties.

claim: The charge of the NP surface containing R384 and E375 may be important for interaction with other protein partners late in the viral life cycle.
source_text: Perhaps the charge of this surface is important for interaction with other protein partners late in the life cycle (after RNA transcription), explaining why E375G is important for growth but not activity.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is a speculative hypothesis to explain the observed differential effects of E375G on growth vs. activity.

claim: E375G is destabilizing.
source_text: E375G is destabilizing, and alone does not rescue growth or activity of R384G.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by stability measurements and functional assays.

claim: Full rescue of viral growth of R384G requires counteraction of NP destabilization and some effect specific to E375G.
source_text: We hypothesize that rescue of growth of R384G requires two events. The first is counteraction of NP destabilization. The second is some effect specific to E375G that is apparent in growth but not transcriptional activity.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from the differential effects observed in activity vs. growth assays.

claim: N334H alone has little effect on activity or growth in the background of the parent Aichi/1968 NP.
source_text: N334H alone has little effect on activity or growth in either background.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The evolutionary trajectory was inferred using a Jones-Taylor-Thornton model of protein substitution.
source_text: We assumed a Jones—Taylor—Thornton model (Jones et al., 1992) of protein substitution, a strict molecular clock and a relatively uninformative coalescent-based prior on the tree.
evidence_reasoning: The claim describes the computational methods used for phylogenetic reconstruction.

claim: Thermal denaturation of NP is irreversible.
source_text: The melting was irreversible (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), preventing us from calculating equilibrium thermodynamic stabilities.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by circular dichroism experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: All NP variants exhibited similar CD spectra with typical alpha-helical characteristics.
source_text: All variants exhibited similar spectra with typical alpha-helical characteristics (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, 3).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: All NP variants unfolded with a single cooperative transition.
source_text: All variants unfolded with a single cooperative transition, allowing us to obtain melting temperatures from sigmoidal curve fits (Figure 6—figure supplements 4–6 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by thermal denaturation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 4–6.

claim: Deletion of residues 2–7 and R416A mutation enable obtaining non-aggregated RNA-free NP in a CD-compatible buffer.
source_text: In order to obtain non-aggregated RNA-free NP in a CD-compatible buffer, we introduced two previously described (Ye et al., 2006) modifications: deletion of residues 2–7 and R416A.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is based on the authors' experimental approach using modifications described in Ye et al., 2006.

claim: M136I can partially rescue the activity of all three individually deleterious mutations.
source_text: In the activity assay, M136I alone has no effect, but it can partially rescue the activity of all three individually deleterious mutations.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: M136I largely rescues the NP protein levels of V280A.
source_text: M136I is present at wild-type levels, whereas levels of V280A are reduced. Adding M136I to V280A largely rescues the NP levels.
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: The two stabilizing mutations N334H and M136I together can rescue the activity of combinations of the individually deleterious mutations.
source_text: Together, the two stabilizing mutations N334H and M136I can rescue the activity of combinations of the individually deleterious mutations (Figure 6—figure supplement 8).
evidence_reasoning: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 8.
